title: Inflation
one_line_summary: Motivates cosmic inflation through the flatness and horizon problems, builds spontaneous symmetry breaking from Landau's theory of a magnet and carries it over to a phi^4 scalar field, derives the Hubble-damped field equation and the scalar-field energy density and pressure in a flat Robertson-Walker universe, uses the slow-roll approximation to obtain exponential growth of a(t), and argues that such expansion drives any initial curvature towards flatness before reheating ends it.
role_in_book: Placed in Part VI directly after the Lagrangian field theory of Chapter 40, this short chapter is the book's first application of that machinery to cosmology. It reaches back to Part III (Robertson-Walker geometry, the Friedmann equations, the de Sitter Universe 1 and Penrose diagrams of Chapters 15-19) and shows that a scalar field with a symmetry-breaking potential behaves like a temporary cosmological constant. It offers an early-Universe story that repairs two weaknesses of the hot Big-Bang model left open in Part III, and it prepares the reader for the status report on inflation and Lambda-CDM in Chapter 49 and the singularity discussion in Chapter 50.

assumed_background.topic: Friedmann equations, density parameter Omega = rho/rho_c and the relation k/adot^2 = Omega - 1
Robertson-Walker metric with k = +1, 0, -1 and its connection coefficients
de Sitter (Universe 1) exponential expansion driven by a cosmological constant, and the Lambda-driven cosh/sinh models
Penrose (conformal) diagrams, light cones at 45 degrees, horizons and the spacelike Big-Bang boundary
Lagrangian density of a scalar field, Euler-Lagrange field equations and the covariant scalar wave equation
Energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field derived from the Lagrangian, and the perfect-fluid tensor
Covariant derivative of a covector via connection coefficients
Helmholtz free energy F = U - TS and equilibrium as a free-energy minimum
Ferromagnets, spins, magnetization and the idea of a critical temperature
Finding stationary points of a function and classifying them with the second derivative
Damped motion of a particle in a potential (friction term proportional to velocity)
Particle-physics energy scales (GeV), unification of forces, the Higgs field and quark confinement at a qualitative level
Cosmic microwave background as a near-perfect blackbody

learning_objectives: Reader can state the flatness problem using k/adot^2 = Omega - 1 and explain why an observed Omega near 1 looks like a fine-tuned initial condition in a decelerating universe.
Reader can explain the horizon problem on a Penrose diagram: two sky directions seen by one observer trace back to events whose past light cones never overlap after the Big Bang.

Reader can describe how an early phase of accelerating expansion 'pushes back' the Big Bang on a conformal diagram so that past light cones overlap, and state the caveat that the shared history can be small.
Reader can distinguish the symmetry of a Hamiltonian from the symmetry of its ground state and explain spontaneous symmetry breaking with the up/down magnet and the buckling Euler strut.
Reader can write Landau's expansion F = F_0 + a M^2 + b M^4, set a = a_0 (T - T_c), and find the broken-symmetry minima M_0^2 = -a/2b below T_c.
Reader can map the Landau free energy onto the phi^4 potential, locate the vacua phi_0 = ±(6 mu^2/lambda)^{1/2}, and classify the stationary points with the second derivative.
Reader can derive phi-double-dot + 3(adot/a) phi-dot + dU/dphi = 0 from the covariant scalar equation using the flat Robertson-Walker connection coefficients, and interpret 3H as Hubble friction.
Reader can extract rho = phi-dot^2/2 + U and p = phi-dot^2/2 - U from the scalar energy-momentum tensor and show that a frozen field acts as an effective cosmological constant Lambda = 8 pi U.
Reader can apply the slow-roll approximation to the coupled field and Friedmann equations to obtain a(t) proportional to exp[(8 pi U_0/3)^{1/2} t].
Reader can derive the acceleration condition p < -rho/3 from the second Friedmann equation, translate it into phi-dot^2 < U, and use it to explain how inflation ends.

Reader can argue from the cosh, exp and sinh Lambda-driven solutions that exponential expansion drives any spatial curvature towards the flat Omega = 1 case, and describe reheating as the hand-off to a standard hot Big Bang.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, analogy-led chapter that borrows its central idea from condensed-matter physics rather than deriving it from cosmology. It opens with two puzzles of the standard hot Big Bang, then spends almost half its length on Landau's theory of a magnetic phase transition, using spin arrays, a buckling strut and double-well free-energy curves to make spontaneous symmetry breaking concrete before relabelling the magnetization as a scalar field. The general-relativistic content is then delivered as one boxed example (the scalar field in a flat expanding universe) and two short deductions: reading energy density and pressure off the field's energy-momentum tensor, and applying slow roll to get exponential expansion. The flatness claim is supported by pointing back to the Lambda-driven Friedmann solutions rather than by a fresh calculation, and the chapter ends with an explicit note that inflation is the dominant but not universally accepted paradigm.
narrative_arc: Epigraph from Alice growing after drinking from the bottle signals sudden enlargement
Motivating puzzle 1: the flatness problem, framed with k/adot^2 = Omega - 1 and the apparent fine-tuning of Omega near unity
Thermal-history interlude (Example 41.1): a cooling Universe passes through GUT, electroweak and confinement phase transitions, planting the idea that phase transitions shape cosmology
Motivating puzzle 2: the horizon problem shown on a Penrose diagram, with events q and r seen by observer p lacking any shared past
Proposed remedy: an early era of accelerating a(t) that pushes the Big Bang back on the diagram; caveat that s and t still share little history; claim that the result is also flat
Model borrowed from condensed matter: Landau's symmetry-breaking phase transition, built from a magnet whose high-T disorder and low-T order are compared under a global 180-degree spin flip
Puzzle of choice: the Hamiltonian treats up and down equally yet the ordered state picks one; the Euler strut shows the same thing mechanically
Formalism for the analogy: Landau free energy as a quartic power series in the order parameter, sign change of a at T_c, minima at ±M_0 (Example 41.2)

Translation to field theory: replace M by phi, F by the potential U of a phi^4 Lagrangian; flip the sign of the quadratic term to obtain two degenerate vacua; mention Higgs mechanism as physical precedent
Cosmological model: phi^4 field with temperature-dependent mu^2(T), uniform in space, evolving in a flat Robertson-Walker spacetime
Derivation (Example 41.3): second covariant derivative of a scalar, flat RW Christoffel symbols, trace with g^{mu nu} gives the equation with Hubble friction 3H
Back-reaction: energy density and pressure of the homogeneous field from T_{mu nu}; frozen field gives rho = -p and an effective Lambda = 8 pi U, recalling de Sitter
Close the system with the k = 0 Friedmann equation; highlight the coupled pair (field equation, expansion equation)
Approximation: slow roll on a shallow potential drops phi-double-dot and phi-dot^2, giving constant H and exponential a(t)
Why flat: compare with the cosh/exp/sinh Lambda solutions, which all approach exponential growth; hence Omega is driven to 1 whatever k was
Exit: acceleration condition p < -rho/3 becomes phi-dot^2 < U; inflation ends when the field speeds up or U falls; oscillation, damping and reheating hand over to ordinary matter and radiation
Status check: inflation is the reigning but not unanimous paradigm; pointer to Chapter 49
signature_moves: Imports a thermodynamic idea (Landau theory) wholesale and then relabels symbols (M to phi, F to U, a to ±mu^2/2, b to lambda/4!) so the double-well picture carries straight into field theory.
Uses paired before/after pictures (spin arrays flipped by 180 degrees) to define 'symmetry of the state' operationally instead of algebraically.
Uses a purely mechanical system, the loaded strut, to show that symmetry breaking needs no quantum mechanics or thermodynamics.
Shows the horizon problem and its cure as a pair of Penrose diagrams that differ only in how far down the Big-Bang line sits.
Gets the cosmological behaviour of the field by reading rho and p off T_{mu nu} and matching to the perfect fluid, turning 'scalar field' into 'fluid with negative pressure' in two lines.
Relies on the reader's stock of earlier exact solutions (de Sitter, cosh/sinh Lambda universes) as the proof of flattening rather than solving new equations.
Keeps the derivation honest but minimal: one boxed covariant calculation, then approximation arguments stated in words.

sections.title: Chapter opening: the flatness problem and the thermal history (Example 41.1)
sections.summary: Recaps that the Universe is modelled as a Robertson-Walker spacetime beginning in a singularity, then rewrites the Friedmann equation as k/adot^2 = Omega - 1. If the Universe is flat, why was it set up that way; if Omega is merely close to one today, that requires a finely tuned past. This is named the flatness problem, with margin pointers to the fine-tuning debate. A second worry, the surprising uniformity of the early Universe, is raised, and Example 41.1 sketches the cooling sequence of early phase transitions (GUT separation near 10^-36 s, electroweak breaking near 10^-11 s, confinement near 10^-5 s).
concepts: phase transitions in the early Universe
key_moves: Friedmann equation recast so that the sign of k is tied to whether Omega is above or below unity
Two readings of Omega near 1: exactly flat forever, or a coincidence requiring tuned initial conditions
Timeline of energy scales and temperatures linking cosmic time to particle-physics phase transitions

sections.title: The horizon problem and the idea of inflation
sections.summary: Regions that could never have exchanged light by the time of an early phase transition are nonetheless seen today at almost identical temperatures. A Penrose diagram makes this concrete: observer p sees events q and r in opposite directions whose past light cones reach the Big Bang without overlapping. The proposed remedy is an early period of accelerating expansion, inflation, which on the diagram lowers the Big-Bang line so that the pasts of q and r, and of events s and t on the transition surface, overlap. The authors caution that s and t still share only a sliver of history, so the horizon problem is eased rather than settled, and state that inflation also flattens space. The key tool announced is the symmetry-breaking phase transition, treated with the field theory of Chapter 40.
key_moves: Define causal disconnection as light not yet having travelled between regions, let alone thermalized them
Contrast inflation's accelerating a(t) with the decelerating solutions studied earlier
Compare two conformal diagrams differing only in the depth of the Big-Bang boundary
Flag Penrose's objection that overlap of pasts may be too slight to guarantee uniformity

sections.title: Symmetry breaking
sections.summary: Develops Landau's picture of a continuous phase transition. Above T_c a magnet's up/down spins are disordered and the zero magnetization survives a global 180-degree flip; below T_c the spins align, the flip reverses M, and the ordered state has lower symmetry than the Hamiltonian, which does not favour either direction. The Euler strut buckling left or right illustrates the same spontaneous choice. Landau expands the free energy in powers of the order parameter; with a = a_0(T - T_c) and b > 0, the single minimum at M = 0 splits into two at ±M_0 below T_c (Example 41.2). The same shape appears in the phi^4 Lagrangian: with a positive quadratic term the vacuum is phi = 0, and with the sign reversed there are two vacua at ±(6 mu^2/lambda)^{1/2}, into which the system rolls. This is the mechanism of the Higgs sector, motivating scalar fields in cosmology.
key_moves: Operational test of symmetry: apply the global flip to the state and ask whether the macroscopic observable changes
Separate symmetry of the Hamiltonian from symmetry of the ground state
Expand F in even powers of M because the energy cannot depend on the sign of M
Let the quadratic coefficient change sign at T_c to generate the transition
Minimize: 2aM + 4bM^3 = 0 gives M_0^2 = -a/2b (Example 41.2)
Identify the field value as the order parameter and U(phi) as the analogue of F
Stationary points of the inverted-mass phi^4 potential and their second derivatives (margin note 11)
Picture the field lowering its energy by rolling down into one vacuum

sections.title: Effective potentials
sections.summary: Introduces the inflating field: a phi^4 field (explicitly not the Higgs) whose mass parameter mu^2(T) changes sign as the Universe cools through T_c, assumed spatially uniform but time dependent. Example 41.3 computes the covariant scalar equation in a flat Robertson-Walker spacetime, finding that expansion adds a friction term 3(adot/a)phi-dot. The energy-momentum tensor gives rho = phi-dot^2/2 + U and p = phi-dot^2/2 - U; a field that is not changing behaves as a fluid with p = -rho, i.e. an effective cosmological constant 8 pi U, recalling de Sitter growth. The k = 0 Friedmann equation with this rho closes the system. Slow roll on a shallow potential makes phi-double-dot negligible and the potential nearly constant at U_0, so the Hubble rate is constant and a(t) grows exponentially.
concepts: second covariant derivative of a scalar
scalar field equation in an expanding universe
energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field
energy density and pressure of a homogeneous scalar field
vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant
key_moves: Temperature enters only through the sign-changing coefficient mu^2(T)
Assume a uniform field so spatial gradients drop out
Use phi_{;mu} = partial_mu phi for a scalar, then one connection term in the second derivative
Only the diagonal of phi_{;mu nu} matters under the trace; Gamma^0_{ii} = a adot supplies the friction
Read rho = T_00 and p = T_ii in the observer's local frame
Match p = -rho to the vacuum fluid to identify Lambda = 8 pi U
Couple field equation and Friedmann equation; drop phi-double-dot and phi-dot^2 under slow roll
Constant H implies exponential a(t)

sections.title: Why flat?
sections.summary: Justifies starting from k = 0 by arguing that inflation erases curvature anyway. The Lambda-dominated Friedmann solutions grow as cosh Ht, exp Ht and sinh Ht for k = +1, 0 and -1, and at late times the hyperbolic functions become exponentials, so every case approaches the flat Omega = 1 behaviour. The acceleration equation shows that positive acceleration needs p < -rho/3, which for the scalar field means phi-dot^2 < U. Inflation therefore stops when the field moves fast enough or the potential falls low enough; a field that reaches its minimum and oscillates is damped to rest, inflation ceasing if the minimum value is not positive, while couplings to other fields drain the field's energy into particles (reheating), leaving a flat universe of matter and radiation. The section closes by calling inflation the reigning but still debated paradigm.
concepts: dilution of spatial curvature by inflation
key_moves: Use the already-known Lambda solutions as proxies for the inflating universe
Asymptotics: cosh and sinh both tend to half an exponential, so curvature becomes irrelevant
Insert rho and p of the field into the acceleration equation to get phi-dot^2 < U
Read the same inequality backwards as the exit criterion
Damped oscillation about the minimum and energy transfer to other fields

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercise
sections.summary: Three bullet points restate the logic: inflation is proposed to cure flatness and horizon problems, it rests on a symmetry-breaking transition as the Universe cools, and slow roll gives a finite stretch of exponential expansion ending in a flat Universe. A single two-part exercise asks for the scalar field equation in a curved (k not zero) Robertson-Walker universe and its reduction to the flat case.
key_moves: Summary ties the three conceptual strands (cosmological puzzles, phase transitions, slow roll) together
Exercise generalizes Example 41.3 to k not zero using the Chapter 16 connection coefficients

concepts.name: flatness problem
concepts.definition: The puzzle that the observed Universe is very close to spatially flat (total density parameter near 1) even though in a decelerating Friedmann universe any departure of Omega from 1 grows with time, so a nearly flat Universe today requires an extraordinarily precise initial value of Omega.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening paragraph: the Friedmann equation is written as k/adot^2 = Omega - 1 and the reader is asked why Omega should be near unity, either because k = 0 exactly or because of a coincidence requiring tuning in the past. The growth of |Omega - 1| is asserted rather than shown.
concepts.notes: Because adot decreases in matter- or radiation-dominated eras, k/adot^2 grows, which is the missing quantitative step (|Omega - 1| grows like a in the matter era and like a^2 in the radiation era). Inflation reverses this since adot grows.

concepts.name: density parameter
concepts.definition: The ratio Omega = rho/rho_c of the total energy density to the critical density rho_c = 3H^2/(8 pi) (G = c = 1); Omega = 1 corresponds to spatially flat k = 0, Omega > 1 to closed and Omega < 1 to open Robertson-Walker geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Part III through eqn 41.1, with the observed value quoted as about 0.3.
concepts.notes: The quoted 0.3 is the matter share only; including dark energy the total is consistent with 1, which is what the flatness argument really concerns.

concepts.name: critical density
concepts.definition: The energy density that makes the Friedmann equation consistent with zero spatial curvature for a given expansion rate: rho_c = 3H^2/(8 pi) in geometrized units.
concepts.how_introduced: Used implicitly in the definition of Omega in the opening; defined earlier in Chapter 17.

concepts.name: fine-tuning of initial conditions
concepts.definition: The worry that a present-day property of the Universe (here Omega near 1) follows only if parameters at early times took values specified to absurd precision, suggesting a missing dynamical explanation.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to make the flatness problem feel problematic, with a margin note pointing to the philosophical literature on fine tuning.
concepts.notes: Inflation replaces a tuned initial value with a dynamical attractor towards Omega = 1.

concepts.name: horizon problem
concepts.definition: The puzzle that regions of the early Universe which, in a decelerating hot Big-Bang model, had no causal contact before the time we observe them (for instance at CMB emission) nevertheless have the same temperature to about one part in 10^5.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in words after noting the surprising homogeneity of the early Universe, then shown on a Penrose diagram in which the past light cones of two events q and r, seen by one observer in different directions, reach the Big Bang without overlapping.
concepts.notes: Book caveat (citing Penrose 2004): inflation gives overlapping pasts but events on the transition surface may share only a small part of their history.

concepts.name: causal connection
concepts.definition: Two regions are causally connected if light (hence any signal) has had time since the Big Bang to pass between them; only then could they interact or thermalize. In the book's Penrose-diagram usage for events q and r, the test is whether their past light cones overlap, i.e. whether they share any history.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 4 defines the phrase in terms of photons having had time to travel between regions, and the Penrose diagram visualizes overlapping or disjoint past cones.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram
concepts.definition: A conformally compactified spacetime diagram in which radial light rays run at 45 degrees and infinities or singularities appear as finite boundaries, so causal relations (which events can influence which) can be read off geometrically.
concepts.how_introduced: Reused from Chapter 19 without re-derivation; the Big Bang is a horizontal line and the effect of inflation is shown by lowering it.
concepts.notes: Lowering the Big-Bang line corresponds to adding a large interval of conformal time before the phase transition.

concepts.name: cosmic microwave background isotropy
concepts.definition: The observation that the CMB has a nearly perfect blackbody spectrum at T = 2.73 K with temperature variations across the sky of only about one part in 10^5.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 2 on the COBE satellite, attached to the claim that the early Universe is surprisingly homogeneous.

concepts.name: phase transitions in the early Universe
concepts.definition: The sequence of symmetry-changing transitions that a cooling, expanding Universe is thought to pass through: separation of the strong from the electroweak interaction at around 10^15 GeV, electroweak symmetry breaking by the Higgs field near 100 GeV, and quark confinement near 100 MeV.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 41.1 lists times, temperatures and energies for each transition as a rough picture, explicitly as the phenomena on which the chapter is built.
concepts.notes: The conversion formula is our addition; with it, 10^15 GeV corresponds to about 10^28 K, a factor of ten above the value printed in Example 41.1.

concepts.name: inflation
concepts.definition: A proposed early phase in which the scale factor accelerates (addot > 0), typically growing nearly exponentially, driven by the potential energy of a slowly evolving scalar field; it drives spatial curvature to negligible values and gives distant regions a shared causal past before a reheating phase starts the standard hot Big Bang.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the remedy for the flatness and horizon problems, illustrated by a modified Penrose diagram, then modelled as a symmetry-breaking scalar field in a flat Robertson-Walker spacetime.
concepts.notes: Attributed in margin note 5 to Alan Guth. The chapter does not discuss the number of e-folds needed or the generation of density perturbations.

concepts.name: accelerating expansion
concepts.definition: Expansion in which the second time derivative of the scale factor is positive, so recession speeds of comoving objects grow; in a Friedmann universe without Lambda this needs p < -rho/3.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted, in a bracketed remark, with the decelerating a(t) of most earlier model universes; quantified in §41.3 via the acceleration equation.

concepts.name: spontaneous symmetry breaking
concepts.definition: The situation in which the laws (Hamiltonian, Lagrangian or free energy) are invariant under a symmetry but the lowest-energy state is not, so the system settles into one of several equivalent ground states related by that symmetry; which one is chosen is fixed by tiny perturbations, not by the laws.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from a magnet: disordered spins keep zero magnetization under a global flip, aligned spins do not. The puzzle of how the system 'chooses' is posed and echoed by the buckling Euler strut, then formalized with Landau's free energy.
formulas: F(M) = F(-M),\quad \text{but ground state } M = \pm M_0 \neq 0
concepts.notes: Margin note 9 stresses that in practice a very small fluctuation tips the system.

concepts.name: global symmetry
concepts.definition: A symmetry transformation applied identically everywhere, for example rotating every spin through the same angle or sending phi(x) to -phi(x) at all points, as opposed to a local (gauge) transformation that may vary from point to point.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after the 180-degree flip of all spins in the magnet, and later for the phi to -phi invariance of the phi^4 potential.
concepts.notes: Local symmetries are the subject of Chapter 44 on gauge fields.

concepts.name: Landau theory of phase transitions
concepts.definition: A phenomenological description of a continuous phase transition in which the free energy near the transition is expanded in powers of an order parameter consistent with the system's symmetry, F = F_0 + a M^2 + b M^4, with a changing sign at the critical temperature; minimizing F gives the equilibrium state on both sides of T_c.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as Landau's way of ignoring microscopic detail: equilibrium balances low energy and high entropy, so minimize F = U - TS written as a power series in M, then take a = a_0(T - T_c).

concepts.name: order parameter
concepts.definition: A macroscopic variable that distinguishes the two phases: its equilibrium (thermal) average is zero on the symmetric, high-temperature side of T_c and takes a non-zero value once the symmetry is broken below T_c. For a ferromagnet it is the magnetization; for a scalar field theory it is the field value phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined while setting up Landau's free energy for the magnet, then reassigned to the equilibrium value of phi(x) when moving to field theory.

concepts.name: critical temperature
concepts.definition: The temperature at which a continuous phase transition occurs; above it the symmetric state is stable, below it the order parameter becomes non-zero. In Landau theory it is where the quadratic coefficient a changes sign.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with the experimental fact that cooling a magnet through T_c produces spontaneous magnetization; later mu^2(T) of the inflaton changes sign at T_c.

concepts.name: free energy minimization
aliases: Helmholtz free energy F = U - TS
concepts.definition: At fixed temperature a thermodynamic system in equilibrium minimizes the Helmholtz free energy F = U - TS, which balances the drive to low internal energy against the drive to high entropy.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as Landau's motivation for studying F rather than energy alone.
concepts.notes: U here is internal energy, not the field potential U(phi) used later.

concepts.name: phi^4 scalar field theory
concepts.definition: A real scalar field with Lagrangian density -(1/2)(partial phi)^2 - U(phi) and potential U = (mu^2/2) phi^2 + (lambda/4!) phi^4 with lambda > 0; it has the global symmetry phi to -phi, a single vacuum at phi = 0 for a positive quadratic coefficient, and two degenerate vacua at phi_0 = ±(6 mu^2/lambda)^{1/2} when the quadratic term is negative.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by transplanting the Landau free-energy shape into the Lagrangian of Chapter 40, splitting off all non-derivative terms as the potential energy density.
concepts.notes: With the sign flipped the potential at its minima is U = -3 mu^4/(2 lambda) < 0; a constant must be added if the true vacuum is to have zero energy.

concepts.name: vacuum of a field theory
concepts.definition: The lowest-energy, spatially uniform configuration of a field, located at a minimum of the potential U(phi); a potential with several degenerate minima has several possible vacua.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when the positive-mu^2 potential has its minimum at phi = 0, and pluralized when the sign flip produces two minima.

concepts.name: Higgs mechanism
concepts.definition: The process in the Standard Model by which a scalar (Higgs) field acquires a non-zero vacuum value as the Universe cools, breaking electroweak symmetry, separating electromagnetism from the weak force and giving mass to the W and Z bosons and to the quarks and charged leptons.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in Example 41.1 as the electroweak transition and after eqn 41.7 as the real-world instance of scalar symmetry breaking, which justifies studying scalar fields in cosmology.
concepts.notes: Margin note 12 warns that the inflating field is not the Higgs even though it is sometimes given that name.

concepts.name: inflaton field
concepts.definition: The hypothetical spatially uniform scalar field whose potential energy dominates the early Universe and drives inflation as it slowly evolves towards a potential minimum.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in §41.2 as a phi^4 field present before the GUT transition, with temperature-dependent mass parameter; the book does not use the word inflaton.

concepts.name: temperature-dependent effective potential
concepts.definition: A potential for the field whose parameters depend on the ambient temperature, here through a quadratic coefficient mu^2(T) that is positive above T_c (symmetric minimum at phi = 0) and negative below it (broken-symmetry minima).
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted in eqn 41.8 with the statement that the cosmic temperature T(t) makes mu^2 change sign in time; no derivation from finite-temperature field theory is given.

concepts.name: second covariant derivative of a scalar
concepts.definition: For a scalar the first covariant derivative is just the gradient; differentiating that gradient covariantly adds one connection term (the ordinary second derivative minus Gamma contracted with the gradient), and contracting the result with the inverse metric gives the wave operator of curved spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed step by step in Example 41.3 for the flat Robertson-Walker metric, keeping only diagonal components because they are all the trace needs.

concepts.name: scalar field equation in an expanding universe
concepts.definition: For a spatially uniform scalar field in a Robertson-Walker spacetime the covariant field equation g^{mu nu} phi_{;mu nu} = dU/dphi becomes phi-double-dot + 3H phi-dot + dU/dphi = 0 with H = adot/a.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Example 41.3 from the Chapter 40 covariant Euler-Lagrange equation, then boxed as one of the two key equations of inflation.
prerequisites: second covariant derivative of a scalar
concepts.notes: For a uniform field the result holds for any k, which is the point of Exercise 41.1.

concepts.name: Hubble friction
concepts.definition: The term 3H phi-dot in the scalar field equation, which acts like velocity-proportional friction on the field's motion in its potential; physically it reflects the dilution of the field's kinetic energy by cosmic expansion.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced before Example 41.3 as a frictional term fixed by the expansion rate, and named an effective drag factor after eqn 41.14.
prerequisites: scalar field equation in an expanding universe
concepts.notes: Large H during inflation is what allows slow roll on a shallow slope; the same term damps the oscillations at the end.

concepts.name: Hubble parameter
concepts.definition: The fractional expansion rate H = adot/a of the scale factor.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the coefficient of the friction term and as the constant rate H^2 = Lambda/3 in the Lambda-driven solutions.

concepts.name: energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field
concepts.definition: The symmetric tensor that a scalar field with kinetic term and potential U contributes as the source of Einstein's equation: the outer product of the field gradient with itself, minus the metric times the Lagrangian-like combination of half the squared gradient plus U (see formula).
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted (from Chapter 40) as the theory's energy-momentum tensor, then evaluated for a uniform field.

concepts.name: energy density and pressure of a homogeneous scalar field
aliases: scalar field as a perfect fluid
kinetic and potential contributions to rho and p
concepts.definition: For a spatially uniform field seen by a comoving observer, rho = phi-dot^2/2 + U and p = phi-dot^2/2 - U: kinetic energy adds to both, potential energy adds to density but subtracts from pressure.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off the time-time and space-space components of T_{mu nu} in the observer's local frame, and compared with the perfect fluid form in margin note 15.
prerequisites: energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field
concepts.notes: Equation-of-state parameter w = p/rho ranges from -1 (potential dominated) to +1 (kinetic dominated); this framing is ours, not the book's.

concepts.name: vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant
concepts.definition: A source with p = -rho has an energy-momentum tensor proportional to the metric and is indistinguishable from a cosmological constant; a scalar field frozen at potential value U therefore acts as Lambda = 8 pi U (G = 1) and drives de Sitter-like expansion.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced by setting phi-dot = 0 in the field's rho and p and comparing with the fluid tensor, then linked to the exponential growth of Universe 1 in Chapter 15.
prerequisites: energy density and pressure of a homogeneous scalar field

concepts.name: Friedmann equation
concepts.definition: The time-time Einstein equation for a Robertson-Walker universe, (adot/a)^2 + k/a^2 = (8 pi/3) rho + Lambda/3 (G = c = 1); with the acceleration equation it governs a(t).
concepts.how_introduced: Used in three guises: rearranged as k/adot^2 = Omega - 1 in the opening, with k = 0 and the scalar rho in §41.2, and as the acceleration equation in §41.3.

concepts.name: slow-roll approximation
concepts.definition: The assumption that, on a sufficiently flat potential with strong Hubble friction, the field's acceleration is negligible (3H phi-dot ≈ -dU/dphi) and its kinetic energy is small compared with U, so that the expansion rate is set almost entirely by the nearly constant potential energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to simplify the coupled equations: a shallow potential below T_c (Fig. 41.7) lets the field creep towards its minimum, making phi-double-dot and phi-dot small.
prerequisites: scalar field equation in an expanding universe
concepts.notes: The standard slow-roll parameters epsilon and eta, which quantify 'shallow', are not introduced.

concepts.name: exponential (de Sitter-like) expansion
concepts.definition: Growth of the scale factor as a(t) proportional to e^{Ht} with constant H, the solution of the Friedmann equation for a constant vacuum energy; for the inflaton H = (8 pi U_0/3)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by integrating the slow-roll Friedmann equation, and compared with the cosh/exp/sinh Lambda solutions of earlier chapters.
prerequisites: vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant

concepts.name: Robertson-Walker spatial curvature index
concepts.definition: The constant k in the Robertson-Walker metric labelling closed (k = +1), flat (k = 0) and open (k = -1) spatial slices.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in the opening and in §41.3, where the three cases are compared under Lambda-driven expansion.

concepts.name: dilution of spatial curvature by inflation
concepts.definition: During near-exponential expansion adot grows, so the curvature term k/adot^2 = Omega - 1 shrinks rapidly; whatever k is, the universe becomes observationally indistinguishable from flat.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued in §41.3 by noting that the cosh (k = +1) and sinh (k = -1) Lambda solutions become exponentials at late times, just like the k = 0 case, and in margin note 16 by noting that curvature effects are too small to matter at the start of expansion.
concepts.notes: The second formula is our explicit version of the book's verbal argument, following from eqn 41.1 with a proportional to e^{Ht}.

concepts.name: condition for accelerated expansion
aliases: violation of the strong energy condition
concepts.definition: In a Friedmann universe without a separate Lambda, addot > 0 requires rho + 3p < 0, i.e. p < -rho/3; for a homogeneous scalar field this becomes phi-dot^2 < U(phi), kinetic energy smaller than potential energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by inserting the scalar rho and p into the acceleration equation, then read as the criterion that decides when inflation stops.
prerequisites: energy density and pressure of a homogeneous scalar field

concepts.name: end of inflation
concepts.definition: The termination of accelerated expansion when the field's kinetic energy becomes comparable with its potential energy or the potential falls to (or below) zero, typically as the field reaches its minimum and oscillates.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by reading the acceleration condition in reverse; margin note 17 adds that a field resting at a positive minimum would inflate forever.

concepts.name: reheating
concepts.definition: The conversion of the inflaton's energy into ordinary particles and radiation through couplings to other fields during or after its final roll and oscillation, which repopulates the empty, cold post-inflationary universe and starts the standard hot Big-Bang evolution.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in bold at the close of §41.3 as the practical way inflation ends, leaving a flat Universe of matter and radiation.

key_equations.name: Friedmann equation in curvature form
key_equations.meaning: The spatial curvature index is tied to the departure of the total density parameter from one; since adot falls in ordinary expansion, any non-zero k makes Omega drift away from 1.
key_equations.symbols: k curvature index; a scale factor; Omega = rho/rho_c

key_equations.name: Landau free energy
key_equations.meaning: Free energy near the transition as an even power series in the order parameter, respecting the M to -M symmetry.
key_equations.symbols: F free energy; M magnetization (order parameter); a, b coefficients (b > 0), possibly temperature dependent

key_equations.name: Temperature dependence of the Landau coefficient
key_equations.meaning: The quadratic coefficient is positive above and negative below the critical temperature, producing the transition.
key_equations.symbols: a_0 positive constant; T temperature; T_c critical temperature

key_equations.name: One-dimensional spin Hamiltonian (margin note 8)
key_equations.meaning: Nearest-neighbour coupling that rewards parallel alignment but has no preference for up over down, showing the symmetry the ordered state breaks.
key_equations.symbols: J coupling constant; S_i^z spin operator of site i along z

key_equations.name: Stationarity of the Landau free energy
key_equations.meaning: Condition for equilibrium states of the magnet.

key_equations.name: Broken-symmetry magnetization
key_equations.meaning: Location of the two minima below T_c (real because a < 0); M = 0 becomes a maximum.

key_equations.name: Scalar field Lagrangian with general potential
key_equations.meaning: Kinetic term plus all non-derivative terms collected into a potential energy density.
key_equations.symbols: (partial_mu phi)^2 = g^{mu nu} partial_mu phi partial_nu phi; U potential energy density

key_equations.name: phi^4 potential
key_equations.meaning: Field-theory analogue of the Landau free energy, symmetric under phi to -phi; single minimum at phi = 0 for positive mu^2.

key_equations.name: Stationary points of the inverted phi^4 potential (margin note 11)
key_equations.meaning: With U = -mu^2 phi^2/2 + lambda phi^4/4!, stationary points lie at 0 and ±(6mu^2/lambda)^{1/2}; curvature is -mu^2 at the origin (maximum) and +2mu^2 at the two minima.

key_equations.name: Broken-symmetry vacua
key_equations.meaning: The two degenerate vacua after the sign of the quadratic term is reversed.

key_equations.name: phi^4 Lagrangian with temperature-dependent mass
key_equations.meaning: Model Lagrangian for the inflating field; mu^2(T) changes sign as the Universe cools below T_c.

key_equations.name: Covariant field equation for the phi^4 field (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Euler-Lagrange equation of (41.8) in curved spacetime.

key_equations.name: Scalar Lagrangian (Example 41.3)
key_equations.meaning: Starting point of the flat Robertson-Walker calculation; identical to (41.5).

key_equations.name: Flat Robertson-Walker inverse metric and connection (margin note 14)
key_equations.meaning: Ingredients for the covariant derivative in a spatially flat expanding universe.

key_equations.name: Covariant scalar field equation
key_equations.meaning: General equation of motion for the scalar in curved spacetime.

key_equations.name: Second covariant derivative of a scalar
key_equations.meaning: Covector rule applied to the gradient of phi.

key_equations.name: Diagonal components in flat RW
key_equations.meaning: Time-time part has no connection term; each space-space part picks up -a adot phi-dot from Gamma^0_{ii}.

key_equations.name: Scalar field equation with Hubble friction (partial-derivative form)
key_equations.meaning: Trace of (41.13) with spatial gradients dropped; expansion supplies a damping term.

key_equations.name: Scalar field energy-momentum tensor
key_equations.meaning: Source term the field contributes to Einstein's equation.

key_equations.name: Scalar field energy density
key_equations.meaning: Kinetic plus potential energy of a uniform field.

key_equations.name: Scalar field pressure
key_equations.meaning: Kinetic minus potential energy; negative when the potential dominates.

key_equations.name: Perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor (margin note 15)
key_equations.meaning: Comparison form: with p = -rho it reduces to -rho g_{mu nu}, a cosmological-constant term.

key_equations.name: Effective cosmological constant of a frozen field
key_equations.meaning: A field not changing in time mimics vacuum energy and can drive de Sitter-type expansion.

key_equations.name: Flat Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: Expansion rate set by energy density when k = 0 and no separate Lambda.

key_equations.name: Friedmann equation for a scalar-field universe
key_equations.meaning: Closes the system by making the expansion rate depend on the field's energy.

key_equations.name: Damped inflaton equation (key equation i)
key_equations.meaning: The field rolls in its potential subject to Hubble friction.

key_equations.name: Expansion equation (key equation ii, corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Restatement of (41.20); together with (41.21) it forms the coupled inflation system.

key_equations.name: Slow-roll field equation
key_equations.meaning: With acceleration neglected, friction balances the potential slope, so the field moves at terminal velocity.

key_equations.name: Slow-roll expansion rate
key_equations.meaning: With small phi-dot and nearly constant U, the Hubble rate is constant.
key_equations.symbols: U_0 near-constant value of the potential during the roll

key_equations.name: Exponential inflation
key_equations.meaning: The scale factor grows exponentially while slow roll holds.

key_equations.name: Lambda-driven expansion for each curvature
key_equations.meaning: All three approach exponential growth at late times, so curvature becomes irrelevant.

key_equations.name: Acceleration equation
key_equations.meaning: Pressure as well as density decelerates expansion; acceleration needs p < -rho/3.

key_equations.name: Inflation condition for a scalar field
key_equations.meaning: Acceleration continues only while the field's kinetic term is below its potential energy; violating it ends inflation.

figures.label: Fig. 41.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two conformal diagrams: (a) without inflation the pasts of q and r, and of s and t on the phase-transition line, never meet; (b) inflation moves the Big Bang far down so these pasts overlap.
figures.visual_description: Two stacked line drawings. Panel (a): a short, wide triangle whose apex is event p; its two 45-degree sides are p's past light cone. Event q sits on the left side and r on the right side, part-way down; the sides end at s (left) and t (right) on a horizontal dotted line marked P.T. A solid horizontal line marked B.B. lies only a hair below the dotted line, so the triangle has almost no room beneath the transition. Panel (b): the same p, q, r, s, t and dotted P.T. line, but the solid B.B. line is moved far down. From s and t long 45-degree lines run down and outward to the new base, making a much larger triangle; from q and r further 45-degree lines descend and cross each other in an X below the P.T. line before reaching B.B., so the past cones of q and r (and of s and t) now share a region. The label B.B. sits at the far left end of the lowered base.
figures.what_it_teaches: The horizon problem is a statement about non-overlapping past light cones, and inflation's effect in conformal time is to lengthen the diagram downward so that widely separated events acquire a common causal past.

redesign.idea: Conformal-time light-cone explorer: a 2D conformal diagram with an observer at the top and two sky points on the last-scattering (or transition) line; a slider adds e-folds of inflation, extending the diagram downward, and past light cones are shaded so their overlap region lights up.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the observer, moves the two emission events apart, and slides the number of inflationary e-folds from 0 to 70; a readout shows the conformal-time depth, whether the cones overlap, and the fraction of shared history.

figures.label: Fig. 41.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Above T_c the spins point randomly up or down, giving zero net magnetization, and flipping every spin leaves that zero unchanged.
figures.visual_description: Two side-by-side grids of vertical arrows, labelled (a) and (b), each five columns across and four rows deep. In (a) the arrows point up or down in an irregular mix with roughly equal numbers of each; (b) is the same grid with every arrow reversed, still an irregular half-and-half mix.
figures.what_it_teaches: A disordered state is invariant (on average) under the global flip, so the high-temperature phase has the full symmetry of the Hamiltonian.

redesign.idea: Live Ising lattice with a temperature slider and a 'flip all spins' button, plus a running magnetization meter.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets T above or below T_c, presses flip, and watches whether the magnetization readout changes; a Monte Carlo update keeps the lattice fluctuating.

figures.label: Fig. 41.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Below T_c all spins line up; reversing every spin turns the all-up state into a distinct all-down state with opposite magnetization.
figures.visual_description: Two side-by-side grids of vertical arrows, five columns by five rows, labelled (a) and (b): in (a) every arrow points up, in (b) every arrow points down.
figures.what_it_teaches: The ordered state is not invariant under the flip, so it has less symmetry than the laws governing it; the two ordered states are equivalent but distinct.

redesign.idea: Merge with Fig. 41.2 into one Ising demo in which cooling through T_c makes domains coarsen until one orientation wins.
redesign.interaction: Learner cools the lattice repeatedly from the same random start with different random seeds and tallies how often up versus down wins.

figures.label: Fig. 41.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A loaded vertical strut is symmetric about its axis but buckles to one side or the other, each outcome breaking the symmetry.
figures.visual_description: Three small sketches, each a hatched elastic column standing on a hatched base with a bell-shaped weight on top. (a) The column is straight and vertical. (b) The column is bent into a gentle S-shaped curve, the weight displaced to one side. (c) The mirror image of (b), bent the other way.
figures.what_it_teaches: Spontaneous symmetry breaking is a generic mechanical phenomenon: symmetric laws and loads, asymmetric outcome, selected by tiny imperfections.

redesign.idea: Buckling strut with a load slider and an adjacent energy-versus-deflection plot that changes from a single well to a double well at the critical (Euler) load.
redesign.interaction: Learner increases the load past critical and adds a tiny left or right nudge (or random noise); the strut buckles and the ball on the energy curve drops into the corresponding well.

figures.label: Fig. 41.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Landau free energy against magnetization: a single well at M = 0 above T_c, a double well with minima at ±M_0 below T_c.
figures.visual_description: Two plots with vertical axis F and horizontal axis M. (a) A U-shaped curve with a flat-bottomed minimum touching the origin. (b) A W-shaped curve: a small hump at M = 0 sitting at the axis, flanked by two symmetric minima dipping below the M axis, then steep walls rising on both sides.
figures.what_it_teaches: Sign change of the quadratic coefficient turns the symmetric minimum into a maximum and creates two equivalent broken-symmetry minima.

redesign.idea: Landau curve with a temperature slider controlling a = a_0(T - T_c) and a second panel showing M_0(T) proportional to (T_c - T)^{1/2}.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags T through T_c; the free-energy curve morphs, a ball settles into a minimum, and the order-parameter curve traces out simultaneously.

figures.label: Fig. 41.6(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The phi^4 potential with a positive quadratic coefficient has one minimum at phi = 0.
figures.visual_description: Plot with vertical axis U(phi) and horizontal axis phi: a steep U-shaped curve with its minimum at the origin, visually identical in shape to Fig. 41.5(a).
figures.what_it_teaches: The field-theory potential has the same form as the Landau free energy; the vacuum is phi = 0 in the symmetric phase.

redesign.idea: Toggle view that overlays the Landau F(M) curve and the phi^4 U(phi) curve with a symbol dictionary (M to phi, a to mu^2/2, b to lambda/4!).
redesign.interaction: Learner flips between 'magnet' and 'field' labels and adjusts the quadratic coefficient; both curves update together.

figures.label: Fig. 41.6(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: With the quadratic term negative the phi^4 potential has a local maximum at phi = 0 and two vacua at ±(6 mu^2/lambda)^{1/2}.
figures.visual_description: Plot with vertical axis U(phi) and horizontal axis phi: a W-shaped double well, central hump at the origin on the axis, two symmetric minima below the axis, and steep outer walls. Exported as a separate image from panel (a).
figures.what_it_teaches: After the sign change the symmetric point is unstable and the field must choose one of two degenerate vacua, whose potential value is below zero for this form of U.

redesign.idea: Double-well sandbox: sliders for mu^2 and lambda show the vacuum positions ±(6mu^2/lambda)^{1/2}, the depth -3mu^4/(2lambda) and the curvature 2mu^2 at the minima.
redesign.interaction: Learner drops a ball near the top with a small random offset and watches which well it falls into; numerical labels update with the sliders.

figures.label: Fig. 41.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: (a) Inflation needs a very shallow potential below the transition; (b) in slow roll the field creeps from near the origin towards the minimum.
figures.visual_description: Two stacked plots of U(phi) against phi. (a) A symmetric potential with steep outer walls but a very broad, almost flat floor that dips only slightly below the phi axis in two faint minima either side of the origin. (b) Only the phi > 0 half: the curve starts at the vertical axis at the axis level, sags very slightly below the axis over a long stretch, then rises steeply on the right. A dashed-outline circle sits at the origin on the vertical axis, and a dotted arrow leads to a grey filled ball resting in the shallow dip.
figures.what_it_teaches: Slow roll is a ball crossing a long, nearly level plateau; the flatness of the potential is what keeps phi-dot small and U nearly constant while the Universe inflates.

redesign.idea: Coupled inflation simulator: numerically integrate phi-double-dot + 3H phi-dot + U' = 0 with H^2 = (8pi/3)(phi-dot^2/2 + U) and show the ball on the potential, phi(t), ln a(t), and a traffic light for phi-dot^2 < U.
redesign.interaction: Learner edits the potential shape (plateau width, depth, lambda), the starting field value and initial velocity; plots update live, counting e-folds and marking when inflation ends and the field oscillates.

worked_examples.label: Example 41.1
worked_examples.problem: Give a rough chronology of the very early Universe in terms of the phase transitions it undergoes as it cools.
worked_examples.method: List successive epochs with cosmic time, temperature and energy scale: unified strong-electroweak interaction near 10^-43 s (10^19 GeV); GUT separation near 10^-36 s (10^15 GeV); Higgs-driven electroweak breaking near 10^-11 s (100 GeV); confinement near 10^-5 s (100 MeV). The box begins on printed p.445 and finishes on p.446.
worked_examples.key_insight: Cosmic history can be read as a cooling curve punctuated by symmetry-breaking transitions, which is why condensed-matter ideas are relevant to cosmology.
worked_examples.result: t ~ 1e-43 s, T ~ 1e32 K, E ~ 1e19 GeV; t ~ 1e-36 s, E ~ 1e15 GeV, T printed as 1e27 K; t ~ 1e-11 s, T ~ 1e15 K, E ~ 100 GeV; t ~ 1e-5 s, T ~ 1e12 K, E ~ 100 MeV
concepts: phase transitions in the early Universe

worked_examples.label: Example 41.2
worked_examples.problem: Locate the equilibrium magnetization below T_c for the Landau free energy F = F_0 + aM^2 + bM^4.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate with respect to M, set to zero, and use a < 0, b > 0 to find real non-zero roots; note the root at M = 0 is now a maximum.
worked_examples.key_insight: Two equal-depth minima appear symmetrically, so the model predicts that a transition must pick one arbitrarily.
worked_examples.result: M_0^2 = -a/(2b); minima at ±M_0, maximum at M = 0

worked_examples.problem: Margin note 11: find and classify the stationary points of U = -mu^2 phi^2/2 + lambda phi^4/4!.
worked_examples.method: Set dU/dphi = -mu^2 phi + lambda phi^3/3! = 0 and evaluate d^2U/dphi^2 = -mu^2 + lambda phi^2/2 at each root.
worked_examples.key_insight: The origin has negative curvature (unstable), the two outer roots have positive curvature 2mu^2 (stable vacua); the same structure as Example 41.2.

worked_examples.label: Example 41.3
worked_examples.problem: Derive the equation of motion for a spatially uniform scalar field with potential U in a spatially flat Robertson-Walker spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Start from the covariant field equation (traced second derivative equals the slope of U). The first covariant derivative of a scalar is its gradient; the second adds a single connection term acting on that gradient. Only diagonal components matter under the diagonal inverse metric. With Gamma^0_{ii} = a adot the space-space components acquire -a adot phi-dot; drop spatial derivatives and contract with g^{tt} = -1 and g^{ii} = 1/a^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Expansion enters the field equation only through a connection coefficient, and it appears as friction proportional to 3H.
concepts: second covariant derivative of a scalar
scalar field equation in an expanding universe

worked_examples.problem: Find the energy density and pressure of a spatially uniform scalar field and determine when it behaves like a cosmological constant.
worked_examples.method: Evaluate T_{mu nu} of eqn 41.15 in the comoving observer's local orthonormal frame with only phi-dot non-zero: T_00 gives rho, T_ii gives p. Set phi-dot = 0 and compare with the perfect-fluid tensor.
worked_examples.key_insight: Potential energy contributes positive density but negative pressure; a static field has p = -rho, which is exactly vacuum energy.
worked_examples.result: rho = phi-dot^2/2 + U, p = phi-dot^2/2 - U; frozen field gives Lambda = 8 pi U
concepts: energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field
energy density and pressure of a homogeneous scalar field
vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant

worked_examples.problem: Solve the coupled field and Friedmann equations in the slow-roll limit.
worked_examples.method: Neglect phi-double-dot so friction balances the potential slope; on a shallow potential near the transition U is approximately a constant U_0 and phi-dot is small, so the Friedmann equation gives a constant Hubble rate, which integrates to an exponential.
worked_examples.key_insight: A nearly constant potential energy acts as a temporary cosmological constant, so the Universe inflates exponentially for as long as the plateau lasts.
worked_examples.result: adot/a ≈ (8 pi U_0/3)^{1/2}; a(t) proportional to exp[(8 pi U_0/3)^{1/2} t]

worked_examples.problem: Find the condition on the scalar field for the expansion to accelerate.
worked_examples.method: Require addot > 0 in addot/a = -4 pi (p + rho/3), giving p < -rho/3; substitute rho and p from eqns 41.16-41.17 and simplify: (2/3)phi-dot^2 < (2/3)U.
worked_examples.key_insight: Acceleration is a contest between kinetic and potential energy of the field, and the same inequality signals the end of inflation.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Up/down spins in a magnet above and below the Curie point
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The disordered and ordered spin arrays are each subjected to a global flip; only the ordered array changes, which defines what it means for a state to have lower symmetry than its Hamiltonian.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The magnet's order parameter is a thermal average over many spins in a lab system with a heat bath; the cosmic field is a single homogeneous classical field whose 'temperature dependence' is put in by hand.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ising lattice demo with a flip-all button and magnetization gauge, linked to the Landau curve.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Euler strut buckling under a load
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A weighted elastic column is perfectly symmetric about its axis yet buckles left or right, with nothing in the physics predicting which; a margin note adds that a tiny imperfection decides.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Purely classical and mechanical, with load (not temperature) as the control parameter; no vacuum energy or cosmological consequence.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Strut with a load slider whose energy landscape morphs from single to double well at the Euler load.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Landau free energy of a magnet as the potential of a scalar field
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The identical quartic shape lets every statement about minima, maxima and symmetry of F(M) be transferred to U(phi), with phi playing the order parameter.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: F is a thermodynamic free energy minimized in equilibrium; U is a term in a Lagrangian whose dynamics include kinetic energy and, in cosmology, Hubble friction, so the field need not sit at the minimum.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Dual-label plot toggling between magnet and field vocabularies.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A ball rolling down a potential with friction
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The field value is pictured as a ball rolling towards a minimum; expansion adds a drag term, and on a shallow slope the ball creeps (Fig. 41.7b).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The 'friction' is not dissipative in the usual sense (energy is diluted by expansion, and its coefficient depends on the field's own energy through H); the ball moves in field space, not physical space.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ball-in-treacle simulation where the treacle viscosity is 3H computed from the ball's own energy.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A static scalar field as a fluid with negative pressure (vacuum energy)
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Matching the field's rho and p to the perfect-fluid tensor shows that potential energy behaves like Lambda, connecting inflation to the already familiar de Sitter model.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only exact when phi-dot = 0; a slowly rolling field has a slowly varying effective Lambda, which is what allows inflation to end.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Equation-of-state dial showing w = p/rho as the kinetic-to-potential ratio is varied, with the region w < -1/3 shaded as 'accelerating'.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Inflating a balloon flattens its surface (implicit in the cosh/sinh argument)
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: dilution of spatial curvature by inflation
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The book argues from late-time asymptotics of cosh and sinh; the standard balloon picture (not in the text) makes the same point geometrically: enormous growth makes a patch of any curved surface look flat.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The balloon is extrinsically embedded and suggests a centre; spatial curvature of an open universe has no balloon picture.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: 3D sphere and saddle patches inflated by a slider while a fixed-size observer's triangle angle sum converges to 180 degrees.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Alice's sudden growth after drinking from the bottle (epigraph)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Sets a playful tone for dramatic, rapid enlargement before the physics begins.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Alice grows inside a fixed room; inflation is expansion of space itself with no container.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Inflation completely solves the horizon problem because all regions now share a causal past.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Inflation makes past light cones overlap, but events on the phase-transition surface may share only a small portion of their history, so uniformity is not automatically guaranteed.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The modified Penrose diagram visibly shows overlapping cones, which looks like a complete fix.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The field that drives inflation is the Higgs field.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The inflating field is a different, hypothetical scalar field; the Higgs mechanism is only an example that scalar symmetry breaking occurs in nature.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both are scalar fields with symmetry-breaking potentials, and some texts loosely call the inflating field a Higgs field.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: When symmetry breaks, the underlying laws must have become asymmetric or something must favour one direction.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Hamiltonian (or Lagrangian) keeps its symmetry; only the ground state lacks it, and the choice among equivalent states is fixed by tiny fluctuations.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In everyday reasoning an asymmetric outcome suggests an asymmetric cause.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Expansion of the Universe always slows down.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The matter- and radiation-dominated solutions decelerate, but a component with p < -rho/3, such as potential-dominated scalar energy, makes addot positive.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Gravity is attractive, and most model universes studied before this chapter decelerate.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Pressure only pushes on walls and plays no role in gravity, so a negative pressure cannot be what makes the expansion speed up.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In general relativity pressure is a source of gravity: addot/a = -4 pi (p + rho/3), so sufficiently negative pressure produces acceleration.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Newtonian intuition pressure is a mechanical force on walls, not a source of gravity, and a uniform pressure exerts no net force.
concepts: vacuum energy as an effective cosmological constant

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Exponential expansion only happens in a spatially flat universe, so starting inflation from k = 0 assumes the answer.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Lambda-driven solutions for k = +1 and k = -1 (cosh and sinh) approach exponential growth too, so the flat outcome is an attractor regardless of initial curvature.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The de Sitter solution usually appears in flat slicing and the chapter's calculation assumes k = 0.
concepts: dilution of spatial curvature by inflation

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Once the field reaches the bottom of its potential, inflation must stop.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: What matters is whether phi-dot^2 < U still holds; a field at rest at a minimum with positive U would keep inflating forever, so a successful exit needs the minimum to have (near) zero or negative energy and the energy to be transferred to other fields.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Rolling to the bottom sounds like the end of the story.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Below T_c the symmetric point M = 0 (or phi = 0) is a metastable state.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is a local maximum, hence unstable: any perturbation sends the system to a minimum. 'Metastable' properly describes a local minimum that is higher than the global one.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book uses the word metastable for this point, and in first-order transitions a metastable false vacuum does exist.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A measured Omega of about 0.3 means the Universe is far from flat.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: About 0.3 is the matter density parameter; adding dark energy gives a total consistent with 1, and spatial curvature is observed to be very small.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter quotes Omega ≈ 0.3 directly beside the flatness relation without saying which components are included.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Inflation means regions moved apart faster than light through space, violating relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Nothing travels through space faster than light; the metric expands, and regions that were once in causal contact are carried beyond each other's Hubble distance.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter describes causally connected regions separating 'rapidly enough', which invites a picture of superluminal motion.

thought_experiments.name: Looking in two opposite directions at the early Universe
thought_experiments.setup: An observer today at event p receives light from events q and r in opposite parts of the sky; trace each event's past light cone back to the Big Bang on a conformal diagram.
thought_experiments.lesson: Without inflation the cones never overlap, so the observed equality of conditions at q and r is unexplained; adding inflation makes the cones intersect.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Draggable sky-point pair on a conformal diagram with an inflation e-fold slider.

thought_experiments.name: Cooling a magnet and asking which way it points
thought_experiments.setup: A magnet with up/down spins is cooled through T_c with a perfectly symmetric Hamiltonian; the reader is asked what decides whether it ends up magnetized up or down.
thought_experiments.lesson: Nothing in the laws decides; a tiny fluctuation selects one of two equivalent ground states, which is spontaneous symmetry breaking.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Repeated cooling runs with random seeds producing a histogram of final magnetization signs.

thought_experiments.name: Perturbing a system poised at the symmetric point
thought_experiments.setup: Prepare the magnet (or field) exactly at M = 0 below T_c and give it the slightest nudge.
thought_experiments.lesson: The state slides into one of the new minima at ±M_0, showing the symmetric point is no longer stable.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Ball balanced on the W-shaped curve with a nudge button.

thought_experiments.name: Inflating a curved universe
thought_experiments.setup: Start a Lambda-dominated universe with positive, zero or negative spatial curvature and let it expand for many Hubble times.
thought_experiments.lesson: The cosh and sinh solutions become indistinguishable from the exponential one, so Omega is driven to 1 whatever the start.
concepts: dilution of spatial curvature by inflation
thought_experiments.app_idea: Three synchronized a(t) curves on a log scale with |Omega - 1| plotted underneath.

historical_notes.event: Developed a general phenomenological theory of continuous phase transitions based on expanding the free energy in an order parameter.
historical_notes.significance: Provides the conceptual template (symmetric laws, broken-symmetry ground state, double-well energy) that the chapter carries over to scalar fields and inflation.

historical_notes.event: Worked out, independently of Chandrasekhar and in 1932, the upper mass limit for a white dwarf supported by degeneracy pressure, as recorded in the biographical margin note.
historical_notes.significance: Shows Landau's direct contributions to relativistic astrophysics beyond condensed matter.

historical_notes.event: Proposed inflation in its original form, studying a scalar field in a universe with flat spatial sections, which is also the setting the chapter adopts.
historical_notes.significance: Origin of the inflationary paradigm; related earlier and parallel work by Starobinsky, Linde, Albrecht and Steinhardt is not mentioned in the chapter.

historical_notes.event: The COBE satellite measured a near-perfect blackbody CMB spectrum at 2.73 K with anisotropies only at the 10^-5 level.
historical_notes.significance: The observational basis for the extreme uniformity that defines the horizon problem.

historical_notes.event: Criticized the claim that inflation fully resolves the horizon problem (cited as Penrose 2004).
historical_notes.significance: The authors present inflation as dominant but contested, preparing the more cautious status discussion of Chapter 49.

applications_and_observations.topic: Uniformity of the cosmic microwave background
applications_and_observations.details: COBE's blackbody CMB with tiny anisotropies is the evidence that causally disconnected regions share the same temperature.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: T = 2.73 K; anisotropy about 1 part in 10^5

applications_and_observations.details: The chapter cites an observational estimate of Omega about 0.3 as not unity but not far from it. This matches the matter component; current data (Planck 2018, external) give total Omega consistent with 1 and curvature parameter Omega_k = 0.001 ± 0.002.

applications_and_observations.topic: Thermal history of the early Universe
applications_and_observations.details: Example 41.1 ties cosmic times to temperatures and energy scales of the GUT, electroweak and confinement transitions.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 1e-43 s / 1e32 K / 1e19 GeV; 1e-36 s / 1e15 GeV (printed 1e27 K; E = k_B T gives about 1e28 K); 1e-11 s / 1e15 K / 100 GeV; 1e-5 s / 1e12 K / 100 MeV

applications_and_observations.topic: Inflation's Hubble rate for a GUT-scale potential (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Our own estimate, not in the book: restoring units, H = (8 pi U_0/3)^{1/2}/M_Pl with M_Pl = 1.22e19 GeV. Taking U_0^{1/4} = 1e15 GeV gives H ≈ 2e11 GeV ≈ 4e35 s^-1, so one e-fold lasts about 3e-36 s and 60 e-folds take roughly 2e-34 s.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: U_0^{1/4} = 1e15 GeV -> H ≈ 4e35 s^-1; 60 e-folds in ~2e-34 s (own estimate)

applications_and_observations.topic: How much flattening inflation provides (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Our own estimate from eqn 41.1: with a proportional to e^{Ht}, |Omega - 1| falls as e^{-2N} after N e-folds. Sixty e-folds suppress an order-one initial curvature by about e^{-120} ≈ 1e-52, enough to offset its later growth during radiation and matter domination.

notation_and_conventions.convention: (-,+,+,+): the flat Robertson-Walker inverse metric has g^{tt} = -1 and g^{ii} = 1/a^2, and the scalar Lagrangian carries -(1/2)(partial phi)^2.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In (+,-,-,-) texts the kinetic term appears with a plus sign.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Geometrized units G = c = 1, so the Friedmann equation reads (adot/a)^2 = 8 pi rho/3 and a frozen field gives Lambda = 8 pi U.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Restore G/c^2 or a Planck mass when making numerical estimates.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The scalar potential energy density is written U(phi), and U_0 is used for the (near-constant) potential value during and at the end of the roll.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Most cosmology literature writes V(phi). U is also used for internal energy in F = U - TS on p.447, a symbol clash.

notation_and_conventions.convention: a and b are the Landau expansion coefficients in §41.1; from §41.2 onward a(t) is the cosmological scale factor.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Clash of symbols; keep them visually distinct when teaching.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The self-interaction is written lambda phi^4/4! so that dU/dphi contains lambda phi^3/3!.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Other texts use lambda phi^4/4, changing the numerical factor in phi_0.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The text keeps mu^2 positive and flips the sign in front of the quadratic term to break symmetry, while the Fig. 41.6 caption says 'mu^2 < 0' yet still writes minima at ±(6mu^2/lambda)^{1/2}.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Pick one convention (e.g. U = -m^2 phi^2/2 + ... with m^2 > 0) when teaching.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Semicolons denote covariant derivatives (phi_{;mu nu}), commas or partial symbols denote ordinary derivatives; for a scalar phi_{;mu} = partial_mu phi.
(partial_mu phi)^2 means g^{mu nu} partial_mu phi partial_nu phi.
Omega = rho/rho_c denotes the total density ratio; k/adot^2 = Omega - 1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The book does not subscript Omega by component here.

notation_and_conventions.convention: H = adot/a; in the Lambda solutions H^2 = Lambda/3.

margin_notes.summary: Epigraph from Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland in which Alice grows until she presses against the ceiling, a whimsical nod to rapid expansion.
The apparent fine tuning of the Universe is much debated; readers are pointed to Lewis and Barnes' book A Fortunate Universe and to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
COBE showed the CMB has a near-perfect blackbody spectrum at 2.73 K with anisotropies of order 10^-5.
The strong-electroweak separation is called the GUT phase transition after the hypothesized grand unified theories.
Explains what 'not causally connected' means here: no photon has yet crossed from one region to the other, so thermal equilibrium between them is out of the question.
Credits Alan Guth with the original proposal of inflation, using a scalar field in a flat universe as the chapter does.
Points to Penrose (2004) for the argument that inflation need not fully solve the horizon problem.
Biography of L. D. Landau (1908-1968): known for condensed-matter foundations, he also contributed to GR, including an independent 1932 derivation of the white-dwarf mass limit.
Gives a nearest-neighbour spin Hamiltonian, -J sum S_i^z S_{i+1}^z, which rewards parallel spins without preferring up or down.
In practice a minute perturbation or fluctuation is what tips a symmetric system into one particular ground state.
Explains that a system prepared at M = 0 below T_c will fall into one of the new minima at the slightest disturbance (the text calls this point metastable).
Works out the stationary points of the inverted phi^4 potential and their second derivatives: maximum at 0 with curvature -mu^2, minima at ±(6mu^2/lambda)^{1/2} with curvature +2mu^2.
Caution: the inflating field is not the Higgs field, although it is confusingly sometimes called one.
The flat-universe simplification is justified in the following section.
Refers to Chapter 15 and Exercise 15.2 for the flat Robertson-Walker connection coefficients Gamma^0_{ij} = a adot delta_ij and Gamma^i_{j0} = (adot/a) delta^i_j.
Recalls the perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor (eqn 41.18) for comparison with the scalar field.
Explains why k = 0 is a safe starting point: at the onset of expansion the effect of k is hard to detect, and treating other k changes predictions by less than observational precision.
Points out the other side of the exit criterion: if the field settles at a minimum where U_0 is positive, the acceleration never switches off and inflation goes on for ever.

difficulty.notes: Mathematically light apart from Example 41.3, which needs comfort with covariant derivatives and Robertson-Walker connection coefficients; the rest is minimizing polynomials and substituting into Friedmann equations. Conceptually it juggles three worlds (cosmological puzzles, condensed-matter symmetry breaking, curved-space field theory) and relies heavily on Chapters 15-19 and 40. The analogies make symmetry breaking accessible, but the slow-roll and flattening arguments are verbal and quick, the quantitative flatness and horizon arguments are missing, and two printed equations (41.9, 41.22) contain slips. The reading copy also drops the double dot on phi in the slow-roll sentence.
