teaching_gems.gem: Define 'the state has less symmetry than the law' by physically applying the symmetry operation to two spin configurations and checking whether the observable changes.
teaching_gems.why_effective: It turns an abstract group-theoretic statement into a before/after comparison a novice can verify by eye.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Spin lattice with a 'flip all' button and a magnetization gauge; at high T the gauge sits at zero before and after, at low T it swings from +M to -M.

teaching_gems.gem: Use the Euler strut to show that symmetry breaking needs no thermodynamics or quantum theory, just a symmetric system past an instability threshold.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A tangible mechanical object removes the mystery and prepares the double-well picture before any equation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Load slider on a 3D elastic column with linked energy landscape that bifurcates at the Euler load.

teaching_gems.gem: Relabel the Landau free energy F(M) as the field potential U(phi), so the magnet's double well becomes the vacuum structure of phi^4 theory.
teaching_gems.why_effective: One picture serves both systems; learners carry intuition about minima and stability straight into field theory.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Morphing curve whose axis labels and coefficient names toggle between magnet and field language while a temperature slider drives the sign change.

teaching_gems.gem: Draw the horizon problem and its inflationary fix as two Penrose diagrams differing only in how far down the Big Bang lies.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Causal overlap becomes a visible geometric fact, and the caveat about s and t is visible in the same picture.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Conformal diagram with an e-fold slider that extends the bottom edge and shades overlapping past light cones.

teaching_gems.gem: Read the field's energy density and pressure straight off T_{mu nu}; with phi-dot = 0 you get p = -rho, so a stuck scalar field is a cosmological constant.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects an unfamiliar field model to the de Sitter universe the reader already knows, in two lines of algebra.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Bar chart of kinetic and potential energy with derived rho, p and w = p/rho, and a de Sitter badge that appears when w approaches -1.

teaching_gems.gem: Show that expansion enters the field equation as friction 3H phi-dot, so inflation is a ball rolling in treacle whose thickness is set by the ball's own energy.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Damped motion is familiar from mechanics, and the self-consistency (H depends on rho) explains why slow roll is self-sustaining.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Side-by-side: ball on potential and phase-space (phi, phi-dot) trajectory flowing onto the slow-roll attractor, with H shown as a changing viscosity.

teaching_gems.gem: Turn the acceleration equation into the single inequality phi-dot^2 < U, which both defines inflation and tells you when it ends.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A compact criterion learners can monitor in a simulation; it makes the exit mechanism a consequence rather than an add-on.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Traffic-light indicator on the inflation simulator that turns red when kinetic energy squared exceeds U, with an e-fold counter that freezes.

teaching_gems.gem: Prove flattening by recalling that cosh Ht and sinh Ht both become e^{Ht}/2 at late times, so all curvature cases converge on the flat solution.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Reuses exact solutions the learner has already met, so the claim is checkable without new calculation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Log-scale plot of three a(t) curves with a companion plot of |Omega - 1| = |k|/adot^2 plunging exponentially.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 41.9 writes the potential derivative as mu^2(T) phi^2 + (lambda/3!) phi^3; the first term should be mu^2(T) phi.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students differentiating U themselves get a mismatch and may doubt their calculus or the field equation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use dU/dphi = mu^2(T) phi + lambda phi^3/3! and point out the slip.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 41.22 has (1/2) phi-dot instead of (1/2) phi-dot^2, contradicting eqn 41.20 which it restates.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Dimensional inconsistency and confusion when coding the coupled equations.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use eqn 41.20; flag 41.22 as a typo.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In the reading copy the slow-roll sentence says phi is negligible; the printed page (rendered) says phi-double-dot is negligible.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Anyone using the text export would think the field itself is set to zero, which contradicts the rolling picture.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Always state slow roll as 'neglect the field acceleration and kinetic energy', never the field value.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The flatness problem is asserted rather than quantified: the text never shows that |Omega - 1| = |k|/adot^2 grows in decelerating eras and shrinks during inflation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may not see why Omega near 1 is surprising, or why inflation is the natural cure.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use eqn 41.1 directly: adot decreases for a proportional to t^{1/2} or t^{2/3}, so |Omega - 1| grows as t or t^{2/3}; for exponential a it decays as e^{-2Ht}. Plot both.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Omega ≈ 0.3 is quoted beside the flatness relation without saying it is the matter density alone; with dark energy the total is consistent with 1.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may conclude the Universe is open and wonder why a flatness problem exists.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Distinguish Omega_m ≈ 0.3, Omega_Lambda ≈ 0.7 and Omega_k ≈ 0, and cite modern curvature bounds (Planck 2018).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The symmetric point M = 0 below T_c is called metastable, though it is a maximum and therefore unstable.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Conflates unstable equilibrium with metastable false vacua, which matter in first-order transitions and old inflation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'unstable equilibrium' for the hump and reserve 'metastable' for a local minimum above the true minimum.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: U_0 is ambiguous: defined as the potential at its minimum after eqn 41.7, then used as the near-constant plateau value that drives inflation, and finally as the minimum again when discussing U_0 < 0. For the pure phi^4 form the minimum value is -3mu^4/(2lambda), which is negative.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: It is unclear what energy actually powers inflation and why a positive vacuum energy is needed during the roll but not afterwards.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Name the plateau value V_inf (powering inflation) separately from the true-vacuum value V_min (which must be close to zero today, hence a constant is added to U).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Fig. 41.6 caption says mu^2 < 0 while giving minima at ±(6mu^2/lambda)^{1/2}, whereas the text keeps mu^2 > 0 and flips the sign of the term.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Imaginary-looking square roots and sign confusion.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Adopt one convention explicitly, e.g. write U = -m^2 phi^2/2 + lambda phi^4/4! with m^2 > 0.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The section titled 'Effective potentials' never derives or explains a finite-temperature effective potential; the sign change of mu^2(T) is simply assumed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the title refers to something they missed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a qualitative note that thermal fluctuations add a term proportional to T^2 phi^2 to the potential, giving mu^2(T) = -m^2 + c T^2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Key modern elements of inflation are absent: number of e-folds (about 60), slow-roll parameters epsilon and eta, quantum fluctuations seeding nearly scale-invariant density perturbations (n_s ≈ 0.965), the tensor-to-scalar ratio and the monopole problem.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The observational case for inflation looks weaker than it is, and the chapter reads as dated relative to CMB-era cosmology.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Supplement with a module on e-fold counting, slow-roll parameters and the primordial power spectrum, linked to Chapter 49.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The link between inflation and the horizon problem is described loosely ('regions separate rapidly enough'); the shrinking comoving Hubble radius, which is the real mechanism, is not introduced.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Invites a picture of superluminal travel and does not explain why accelerating expansion (not just fast expansion) is required.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Plot the comoving Hubble radius 1/(aH) versus ln a: it falls during inflation and rises afterwards, so modes exit and later re-enter the horizon.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 41.1's thermal history is loose: 10^15 GeV corresponds to about 10^28 K rather than 10^27 K; 10^19 GeV is the Planck scale, where gravity is expected to join in; and the Higgs gives mass to the W and Z bosons and to quarks as well as charged leptons, not only to some leptons.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Numbers may be copied into estimates, and the particle-physics picture is slightly misleading.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use E = k_B T (1 GeV ≈ 1.16e13 K) and describe the electroweak transition more precisely.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Symbol clashes: U means internal energy in F = U - TS and potential energy density later; a is a Landau coefficient and then the scale factor; T is temperature and T_{mu nu} the energy-momentum tensor.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Momentary confusion when the chapter moves from §41.1 to §41.2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Rename in teaching materials (e.g. E_int, V(phi), alpha for the Landau coefficient).

tutor_notes: Open with a puzzle rather than a definition: 'Two patches of the CMB on opposite sides of the sky never had time to exchange a photon, yet their temperatures agree to 1 part in 100,000. How could that be?' Then ask separately why the Universe should be so close to flat.
Check prerequisites first: can the learner write the Friedmann equation, say what Omega and k mean, and read a light cone on a Penrose diagram? If not, detour to GA ch17 and ch19 before continuing.

Order of explanation that works: (1) the two puzzles, (2) symmetry breaking with the magnet and strut, (3) double-well potential and field language, (4) field in an expanding universe with Hubble friction, (5) rho and p and the Lambda connection, (6) slow roll and exponential growth, (7) why curvature is erased, (8) how inflation ends and reheating.
Understanding check for symmetry breaking: 'Does the Hamiltonian of the magnet change below T_c?' The correct answer is no; only the ground state loses the symmetry.
Understanding check for vacuum energy: ask the learner to compute rho and p for phi-dot = 0 and to say what fluid behaves like that. Expected: p = -rho, a cosmological constant.
Understanding check for acceleration: 'Why does negative pressure make the Universe speed up rather than slow down?' Guide them to addot/a = -4 pi (p + rho/3): pressure gravitates in GR.

When teaching Example 41.3, have the learner compute only the diagonal of phi_{;mu nu} and the single connection coefficient that matters (Gamma^0_{ii} = a adot); insist they track the sign from g^{tt} = -1.
Warn about the printed slips: eqn 41.9 should have mu^2 phi, not mu^2 phi^2, and eqn 41.22 should contain phi-dot squared.
Common learner question: 'Is the inflaton the Higgs?' Answer: no, it is a separate hypothetical field; the Higgs only shows that scalar symmetry breaking happens in nature.
Common learner question: 'Did inflation make things move faster than light?' Answer: no local motion exceeds c; space expands, and the comoving Hubble radius shrinks during acceleration.

Common learner question: 'If the bottom of phi^4 is negative, doesn't that give a negative cosmological constant today?' Acknowledge the point and explain that a constant is added so the true vacuum has (nearly) zero energy.

For advanced learners, extend with e-fold counting (N = integral of H dt ≈ 60), slow-roll parameters, and quantum fluctuations as the seeds of structure; for beginners, stop at the ball-on-a-plateau picture and the phi-dot^2 < U criterion.
Be candid about status: inflation is the dominant paradigm and matches CMB data well, but it is not universally accepted, and the chapter itself signals this (see GA ch49 §49.8).
